posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I'm thinking of building a portable table construction. The idea is to make a steel frame that can hold several (for example 50x50cm) tiles on top of the frame, and a wooden tray on a lower level that I can fill will stones or sand to make the table heavy. I will support the legs of the frame on air filled tires.

Now I am afraid that, because the table top will be segmented because of the tiles, that this might cause stability problems. Otherwise I could perhaps order a one-piece thinner sheet of steel that is more portable than the usual 1/2 inch steel plate.

Would this be a workable solution? Or does the actual table top have to be one thick heavy peace?

(p.s. my TEC controller design is almost finished I will start a website when it is done. It will also feature a mini-servo controlled shutter/timer, next step...open source holographic plates)

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
I like the part about using a steel framework to support the table. That's what I use (square, perforated steel pipe, with threaded tie-rods going through some of them, tightened firmly on the ends with bolts).

Personally I wouldn't use a segmented table top. I use a single piece of granite. Although it's the thin variety (about 1 inch thick), it's well-supported underneath by the steel framework. It's the kind of granite used for kitchen counters, and since it's reasonably thin, the weight is much more manageable (compared to thicker granite). Personally, I don't like steel because of its greater expansion/contraction with temperature changes (for long exposures, that is). I use gravity mounts for the optics. The mounts don't need to be heavy, just flat on the bottom so they don't wobble (three-point supports could be used also). The top surface of the granite should already be flat and smoothly polished.

For legs, I bolt 2-inch galvanized pipe (for plumbing) to the steel framework (the legs are 3 feet long in my case). For vibration isolation, I put a racquetball under each leg. (I needed to put a fixture on each end of the legs, so that the racquetballs wouldn't creep up into the pipe over time.) Racquetballs are pressureless, and don't need to be re-filled with air. I would use as many legs as necessary to provide plenty of support for the steel framework.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: I would not recommend a segmented table top. Although it *will* work (if constructed by someone experienced with interferometric stability issues), the uncertainty about its integrity when built as a first table would (I think) outweigh its portability. Instead, I'd recommend a layer of interlocking cinder blocks (tied together by threaded rods through their holes), supported by a sheet of 3/4" plywood, and topped with a sheet of 1/8" steel. While not portable, this construction comes apart in pieces easily managed by two people.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Many interesting setups can be made on a 1' x 1' table. Take a piece of graph paper and layout some setups before construction of your table. Bigger is more fun but many people have done great things with small tables.

My next table will be 4'x8' but I could probably do everything on my 3'x6' table if I had to.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hans, Danny came up with a very good idea about a table some time back.

Find an steel door that has a little weight to it (100lbs US or so). Then simply place this door on inner tubes.

I have not tried it but steel doors are very rigid, very available, cheap and easy to move. I guess the biggest downfall would be the relatively light weight. Maybe you could build your wood frame stone filled shell and then place a steel door on top for additional rigidity and a nice flat top.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md:
Lon Moore was one of the most prolific holographers ever. He ran his lab in different incarnations from 1971 to 2003. He prefer ed to master on a sand table even though he had a very nice newport table.

His take on sand was there was not a long settle time once you learned how to place the optics. He said that you acquire a feel for how to insert the mount in the sand.

It is a shame that this generation of amateur holographers has not adopted sand tables. They work very well.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md: I tried a new approach to sand tables just before I moved into the lab that I am in now. About 9 months ago. I had a sand table and my mounts are made out of a weighlifting set. Big round bases. You can see them on my web page under new lab. I took the dark green contractors trash bags (the thick ones - I think 6 mil thick) and put them on the top of the sand and duct taped them together. When I would set a optic, I would place it where I wanted and tap the top, a little hard at first and gradually easier. I could feel it set in the sand through the plastic liner. This worked very well and kept the sand dust down when moving optics.
